name: Dietary fibre supplements (by mouth)
short: Guar gum diet tablets: 25 gullet or bowel blockages, 2 reported deaths (1 after surgery). Psyllium cases: blockage; anaphylaxis if sensitised. Trials: more wind. Soluble fibre may cut drug absorption.
text: Serious harms come from case reports and reviews of individual fibres. A case report describes blockage of the oesophagus by a mass of psyllium husk powder in a 76-year-old man with Parkinson's disease, and another describes intestinal obstruction in a 26-year-old man after eating psyllium-containing diet food, with the authors warning that obstruction may occur if psyllium is taken without adequate fluid. A 1980 case report describes small-bowel obstruction requiring surgery in an elderly nursing-home resident who had taken excessive amounts of a bulk laxative for many years; a colon cancer was probably the immediate cause. A review of bezoars formed from medicines (solid masses in the gut) lists guar gum and psyllium preparations among the causes and says such masses most often occur in people with altered gut motility or anatomy. An analysis of 26 reports of suspected adverse reactions to a guar gum diet tablet, sent to the United States regulator, found 18 cases of oesophageal obstruction, seven of small-bowel obstruction, and one person reported to have died after taking it for whom too few details were given to assess whether the tablet caused the death. One patient with oesophageal obstruction died after developing a pulmonary embolism following surgical repair of a tear in the oesophagus made during rigid endoscopy to remove the blockage. Half of those with oesophageal obstruction had earlier oesophageal or stomach disorders. Case reports describe severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, after swallowing psyllium in people already sensitised to it, such as nurses who had handled it. In trials in adults with chronic constipation, a 2022 meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials and a 2016 meta-analysis of 7 found more flatulence with fibre than with control or placebo, and the 2016 authors say fibre causes moderate gastrointestinal side effects, while rating the evidence low quality. In children, the 2018 meta-analysis of 9 trials (680 children) gives no adverse-event data in its abstract; in a double-blind trial in 135 children randomised to a fibre mixture or lactulose for 8 weeks, abdominal pain and flatulence scores were comparable and no serious adverse effects were registered. Interactions: a review of herb-drug interactions states that soluble fibres, including guar gum and psyllium, can decrease the absorption of drugs. In a double-blind study in 10 healthy volunteers, guar gum significantly lowered the peak blood level of phenoxymethyl penicillin and the area under its blood-level curve, and lowered blood digoxin levels during early absorption, although a similar amount of digoxin was found in 24-hour urine with or without guar gum. In 6 healthy volunteers given metformin together with guar gum, the rate of metformin absorption was reduced over the first 6 hours, and the authors suggest this may diminish metformin's blood-sugar-lowering action. These studies are of guar gum, one type of fibre.
